title: A Spectral Identifiability Threshold for Dissipative Rate Recovery from Truncated Liouvillian Spectra
abstract: Open quantum systems lose energy and phase coherence through different dissipative processes, but these processes can produce overlapping dynamical signatures. The Liouvillian spectrum summarizes how such a system relaxes, yet it is not obvious how much of that spectrum is needed to distinguish the underlying dissipation rates. We study this question for amplitude damping and dephasing in a six-qubit Lindblad model whose spectrum can be derived analytically. We retain only the slowest non-steady spectral modes and ask how many are required before each dissipative rate becomes recoverable. We show that population modes contain no dephasing information, which creates a lower bound of D = 2^n retained modes for uniform dephasing identifiability in the relevant rate regime. The measured recovery threshold reaches this bound at n = 4,5,6, while n = 3 remains above it. At n = 6, least squares achieves a mean joint absolute error of order 10^-9, compared with 4.355 x 10^-4 for four tabular learning methods. Robustness tests show that this advantage weakens when the spectra are perturbed and when a transverse field breaks the commuting structure. These results show that the amount and structure of retained spectral information can determine whether dissipative parameters are recoverable, independently of the estimator used. The present conclusions apply to noise-free simulator spectra rather than measurement-derived spectra.
summary: This paper determines the minimum number of spectral modes needed from a truncated Liouvillian spectrum to accurately recover the underlying energy and dephasing rates of an open quantum system. By establishing a spectral identifiability threshold, it shows that the amount and structure of retained spectral information dictates parameter recoverability, independent of the estimator used.
main_problem: The paper addresses the fundamental question of determining the minimum amount of spectral information (spectral depth) required to uniquely recover underlying dissipative rates from a truncated Liouvillian spectrum.
main_result: A quantifiable spectral identifiability threshold ($k^\star$) is established, showing that for a six-qubit system, the recovery of dephasing rates saturates a theoretical lower bound derived from the population sector.
method: The study uses a supervised inverse benchmark, fitting the dissipative rates ($\gamma_1, \gamma_\phi$) by regressing against the sorted real parts of the slowest non-steady Liouvillian eigenvalues, comparing linear regression to various machine learning models.
model_or_system: The model is a synthetic six-qubit open quantum system governed by a Lindblad master equation, analyzed in the Markovian regime. The Liouvillian spectrum eigenvalues are analytically related to the dissipative rates.
key_observables: Dissipative rates ($\gamma_1$ for amplitude damping and $\gamma_\phi$ for dephasing), and the Mean Absolute Error (MAE) of the recovered rates.
important_parameters: The spectral depth ($k$, number of retained slow modes) and the system size ($n$, number of qubits).
main_assumptions: The conclusions are strictly limited to noise-free simulator spectra, not spectra derived from actual quantum measurements.
figures_summary: Figures schematically illustrate the model, the Liouvillian spectrum, the sorted spectral features, and the recovery error as a function of the retained spectral depth $k$.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the physical model, derives the analytical form of the eigenvalues, defines the inverse problem (rate recovery from truncated spectrum), performs quantitative benchmarking across various spectral depths, and compares the results against theoretical lower bounds.
why_interesting: This work provides rigorous, quantitative bounds on the information content required to characterize open quantum dynamics, which is crucial for designing optimal quantum measurement protocols or tomography schemes.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks
